--- title: "Repeat & package: loops, matrices, functions" subtitle: "The R Statistical Language · Session 3" format: revealjs: footer: A. Stamm · The R Statistical Language · Session 3 knitr: opts_chunk: echo: true --- # Welcome back ## Where we left off {.inv} You can already *explore* a dataset: shape it with the pipe and `dplyr`/`tidyr`, and read it back with ggplot2's grammar. ::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly} - the [pipe]{.green} `|>` and the `dplyr`/`tidyr` verbs (`filter`, `select`, `mutate`, `arrange`, `group_by`/`summarise`); - [base-R plots]{.green} and [ggplot2]{.amber}: histograms, scatters, facets, boxplots; - the [transform → plot → interpret]{.indigo} EDA loop. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **The move today.** Your EDA loop is full of moves you repeat: grouped summaries, reshapes, simulations. This session looks *underneath* them: we leave the tidyverse and work in base R, replacing copy-paste with loops, reaching into two dimensions with matrices, and turning the moves you repeat into reusable functions you keep. ::: ## Today's map {.inv} ::: {.session-arc}
1Foundations
2Explore your data
3Repeat & package
::: Session 3 is the **"repeat & package"** move of the course: stop doing by hand what R can do by itself: ::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly} - [repeat & branch]{.green}: [loops]{.green} (`for`, `while`) and conditionals (`if/else`, `ifelse`); - [reach 2D]{.amber}: [matrices]{.amber}, the vector's 2D cousin, plus linear algebra and `apply`; - [package the logic]{.indigo}: [writing your own functions]{.indigo}, scope-aware, vectorised, tested. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **The thread.** The Monte-Carlo experiment ties the session together: we *loop* over thousands of samples, and we *package* that loop into one reusable, tested function. Matrices give us the two-dimensional structures the algebra often lives in. ::: # Loops and conditionals ## The problem loops solve {.inv} Often you want to repeat the same step on many things: - your function models ten species; - you average over 1000 simulations; - you transform every column of a table. You could copy-paste... or you let **R repeat for you**. ## `for` loops {.inv} Repeat a block a fixed number of times: the body runs once per value: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} A simple `for` loop ```r for (i in 1:5) print(i^2) # i takes each value of the sequence in turn total <- 0 # the body runs once per value for (x in c(2, 4, 6, 8)) total <- total + x total # 20 ``` ::: ::: {.paper-card} Afterwards `i` is a normal variable: it still holds the loop's last value. ::: ## Pre-allocate for speed {.inv} Growing a vector inside a loop is slow. **Pre-allocate** the result first: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} Pre-allocate, then fill by index ```r n <- 1000 out <- numeric(n) # a vector of n zeros, ready to fill for (i in 1:n) { out[i] <- rnorm(1) } ``` ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **Rule of thumb.** Decide the output's length *before* the loop, create the container, then fill slots by index (`out[i] <- ...`). This is much faster than `out <- c(out, ...)` inside the loop, a habit that matters once your data grows. ::: ## `while` loops {.inv} Repeat *while a condition holds*: useful when you don't know the number of steps in advance: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} A `while` loop ```r x <- 1 while (x < 1000) { x <- x * 2 } x # 1024 ``` ::: ::: {.callout-caution title="Guard against infinite loops"} If the condition never becomes `FALSE`, the loop runs forever. Always make sure something inside the body moves toward stopping the loop. ::: ## Conditionals: `if` / `else if` / `else` {.inv} Branch on a condition: only **one** branch runs: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} `if`/`else` is an expression: it hands a value back ```r score <- 82 grade <- if (score >= 90) "A" else if (score >= 80) "B" else "C" ``` ::: ::: {.callout-caution title="Long vectors break `if`"} `if` needs a *single* `TRUE`/`FALSE`: use `ifelse()` for vectors. ::: ## Element-wise choice: `ifelse` {.inv} For **vectorised** decisions, use `ifelse(condition, when_true, when_false)`: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} Element-wise choice with `ifelse` ```r temps <- c(-2, 15, 28, 33) ifelse(temps > 25, "hot", "not hot") ``` ::: It applies the branch *element-wise* to a whole vector: no loop needed. This is the idiomatic replacement for "for each value, choose one of two things". ::: {.callout-desc} **`if` vs `ifelse`.** Use `if/else` to choose *which block of code* runs once; use `ifelse` to map a *vector* to one of two values. Mixing them up is a classic beginner bug. ::: ## Which tool when? {.inv} ::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly} **`for`**: repeat a block a *known* number of times (fill a pre-allocated vector, iterate over columns). **`while`**: repeat *until a condition* flips (unknown count of steps). **`if/else`**: choose *one block of code* based on a condition. **`ifelse`**: map a *vector* element-wise to one of two values. **`*apply` family**: "loop over each element and apply a function" (met in Session 1 with lists, and again below with matrices). ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Often the *cleanest* loop is no loop at all: vectorization, `ifelse`, or `lapply`/`vapply` are simpler than an explicit `for`. ::: ## The `*apply` family: loop & apply {.inv} Say "**apply this function to every element**" instead of writing the loop by hand: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} lapply, sapply, vapply ```r l <- list(a = 1:3, b = 4:6) lapply(l, mean) # a list back — keeps the original structure sapply(l, mean) # tries to simplify: a named vector vapply(l, mean, 0) # like sapply, but you promise the output type ``` ::: ::: {.paper-card} The family you first met on lists in **Session 1** (and will meet again on matrices as `apply`, `MARGIN = …`): `lapply` always, `sapply` when simple, `vapply` when you want the guarantee. It's "loop, *then* apply" collapsed into one verb. ::: ## Grouped summaries in base R {.inv} `group_by |> summarise` (Session 2) has a base-R cousin that returns the split-by-group result directly: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} tapply & aggregate, base R ```r tapply(penguins$body_mass_g, penguins$species, mean, na.rm = TRUE) # Adelie Chinstrap Gentoo # 3700.7 3733.1 5076.0 aggregate(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins, FUN = mean) ``` ::: ::: {.paper-card} `tapply(vector, group, fun)` summarises by group; `aggregate(formula, data, fun)` returns a tidy `data.frame`. When your pipeline gets more steps, reach for the `dplyr` verbs; when it's one grouped summary, these one-liners are hard to beat. ::: ## Your turn: loops & conditionals {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} 1. `for` loop printing squares of `1:10`. 2. Loop-sum `1:1000`; confirm it equals `sum(1:1000)`. 3. Given `temps <- c(-5, 4, 12, 25, 31)`, use `ifelse` to label `"freezing"`…`"hot"` by thresholds of your choice. 4. **Monte-Carlo**: average 5000 samples of `rexp(30)` into a pre-allocated vector, then `hist()` it: bell-shaped despite the exponential source? ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **Lab 1: loops (≈25 min).** Continue in `lab-1-loops.R`. The Monte-Carlo in Q4 is our Central Limit Theorem *by simulation*: no theorem needed, just loops and histograms. ::: # Matrices ## What is a matrix? {.inv} A **matrix** is a *two-dimensional rectangular array* of **one type** (usually numeric): a vector folded into rows and columns. It's the **2D cousin of the vector**. ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} Build and subset a matrix ```r m <- matrix(1:12, nrow = 3, ncol = 4) # vector -> rows & columns m[2, 3] # subset with [row, col], like a data frame dim(m) # 3 4 nrow(m); ncol(m) # 3 4 ``` ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **Key distinction.** A data frame is a *list of columns* (columns may differ in type); a matrix is *one vector in 2D* (single type). For tabular *data* with mixed types, prefer a data frame/tibble; reach for a matrix when you need **linear algebra**. ::: ## Building & reshaping {.inv} A matrix is just a vector with a `dim` (dimension) attribute, so you can build or reshape them freely: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} `matrix()`, `rbind`/`cbind`, and `dim()` ```r A <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3) # column-major fill identical(A, rbind(1:3, 4:6)) # TRUE — cbind/rbind by row cbind(A, c(7, 8)) # add a column dim(A) <- NULL # strip the dim -> back to a vector ``` ::: ::: {.callout-caution title="Column-major by default"} `matrix()` fills **column by column** unless you pass `byrow = TRUE`. A classic source of "why is my matrix transposed?" surprises. ::: ## Arithmetic & recycling {.inv} Element-wise arithmetic works like it does on vectors, and **recycling** applies: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} Arithmetic on a matrix ```r M <- matrix(1:6, 2, 3) M * 2 # scalar multiplies every entry M + c(10, 20) # length-2 vector recycles down the COLUMNS M * matrix(c(1, 10), 2, 1) # column vector scales each column ``` ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **Watch the recycling axis.** A length-2 vector recycles along columns (down), not across: get this wrong and your standardisation silently miscalculates each column. ::: ## Linear algebra {.inv} Matrices exist to do **algebra**: matrix product, transpose, inverse, determinant: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} Matrix algebra ```r A <- matrix(c(2, 4, 1, 3), nrow = 2) # a 2x2 A %*% A # matrix product t(A) # transpose solve(A) # inverse det(A) # determinant diag(4) # 4x4 identity ``` ::: ::: {.callout-caution title="`%*%` is not `*`"} `A * B` is **element-wise**; `A %*% B` is the **matrix product** (rows × columns). Absent the right dimensions, `%*%` errors, which is usually the clue you wanted a matrix, not a data frame. ::: ## Fold a data frame into a matrix {.inv} Any rectangular **numeric** block can be coerced to a matrix when algebra needs it: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} `as.matrix()` for numeric tables ```r nums <- iris[, 1:4] # 150 x 4, all numeric M <- as.matrix(nums) # data frame -> matrix dim(M) # 150 4 class(M) # "matrix" "array" ``` ::: ::: {.callout-desc} `as.matrix()` forces everything to **one type**: if any column is character, the whole matrix becomes character. Check `str()` before you coerce, and keep a real data frame for mixed-type data. ::: ## Row/column summaries & `apply` {.inv} Summarise along one axis with the `row*`/`col*` helpers, or generalise with `apply`: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} rowSums, colMeans, and apply(MARGIN) ```r M <- matrix(1:12, 3, 4) rowSums(M); rowMeans(M) # per row (MARGIN = 1) colSums(M); colMeans(M) # per column (MARGIN = 2) apply(M, 1, sd) # sd of each row apply(M, 2, function(x) max(x) - min(x)) # range of each column ``` ::: ::: {.callout-desc} `apply(M, MARGIN, fun)`: `MARGIN = 1` goes down rows, `MARGIN = 2` across columns. It's `lapply`'s 2D sibling: a loop over one axis hidden inside a one-liner. ::: ## Standardise a matrix (full example) {.inv} Let's **z-score** every column of a matrix, the machinery behind a real analysis: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} Column-wise z-scoring ```r M <- matrix(c(1, 100, 2, 200), 2, 2) mu <- colMeans(M) # mean of each column sig <- apply(M, 2, sd) # sd of each column Z <- sweep(M, 2, mu, "-") # subtract each column's mean Z <- sweep(Z, 2, sig, "/") # divide each column's sd colMeans(Z) # ~ 0 apply(Z, 2, sd) # ~ 1 ``` ::: ::: {.callout-desc} `sweep(M, MARGIN, vector, FUN)` applies a function across one axis, here subtracting a column mean. This is the pattern `scale(M)` automates; you now see what's underneath. ::: ## Your turn: matrices {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} 1. Build `matrix(1:20, 4, 5)`; report `dim`, `rowSums`, `colMeans`. 2. Transpose it with `t()`; what happens to the dimensions? 3. `A <- matrix(c(4, 2, 1, 3), 2, 2)`: compute `A %*% solve(A)`; what should you get? `det(A)`? 4. Standardise the columns of `iris[, 1:4]` (as a matrix) so each column has mean 0, sd 1. Check with `colMeans` / `apply(., 2, sd)`. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **Lab 2: matrices (≈20 min).** In `lab-2-matrices.R`. Standardising by hand is the kind of thing you'll later hand to a *function*, which is exactly the next section. ::: # Writing custom functions ## Why functions? {.inv} Copy-pasting code is how bugs multiply. A **function** lets you: - name a block of logic so its *intent* is readable; - reuse it with different inputs; - fix a bug **once** instead of in every copy. Any analysis you do more than twice deserves a function. ## Anatomy of a function {.inv} ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} The anatomy of a function ```r function_name <- function(arg1, arg2 = default) { result <- ... # body: work on the arguments return(result) # hands a value back } ``` ::: ::: {.paper-card} - **name**: how you call it; - **arguments**: inputs (optionals get defaults); - **body & return**: code that runs & value handed back. ::: ## Scope: what the body sees {.inv} Variables created *inside* a function live **only there**: they don't leak out: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} What the body sees ```r g <- function(x) { internal <- x * 2 # exists only inside the call internal + 1 } g(5) # 11 ``` ::: ::: {.callout-caution title="Lexical scoping"} A function *can* see variables from the outside, but relying on that is fragile: pass everything it needs as **arguments**. Explicit inputs in, explicit output out, is what makes functions testable and reusable. ::: ## Functions wrap loops {.inv} The Monte-Carlo from the loops section is a loop crying out to be a function: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} Turn the loop into a function ```r clt_sim <- function(n = 30, R = 5000) { means <- numeric(R) for (r in 1:R) means[r] <- mean(rexp(n)) means } hist(clt_sim()) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **The payoff.** The loop from "Your turn: loops" is now a *named, reusable, parameterisable* tool: `clt_sim(n = 100)` measures the same CLT with bigger samples, no copy-paste. ::: ## Vectorised functions & defaults {.inv} Functions are **vectorised**: they work element-wise on vectors: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} Vectorised with defaults ```r f_to_c(c(32, 212, 98.6)) # works on the whole vector clamp <- function(x, lo = 0, hi = 1) # defaults → optional args ifelse(x < lo, lo, ifelse(x > hi, hi, x)) clamp(c(-1, 0.5, 2)) # 0.0 0.5 1.0 ``` ::: ::: {.paper-card} `ifelse` in the body: the element-wise tool from earlier, and the vectorised `clamp` needs no loop at all. ::: ## When functions aren't vectorised: `Vectorize()` & `replicate()` {.inv} Built-in functions are usually vectorised, but your own (or a third-party) function may only accept **one scalar at a time**. Two loop-free helpers: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} `Vectorize()` wraps a scalar function so it takes a vector; `replicate()` repeats an expression ```r # not vectorised: takes one date string parse_it <- function(x) strsplit(x, "-")[[1]][1] parse_it(c("2024-05-01", "2024-06-15")) # only the first is parsed parse_all <- Vectorize(parse_it) # wraps it => element-wise parse_all(c("2024-05-01", "2024-06-15")) set.seed(7) replicate(4, mean(rexp(10))) # repeat an expression R times ``` ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **Loops without loops.** `Vectorize()` turns a scalar-only function into a vector one; `replicate(R, expr)` re-runs an expression `R` times and collects results, the function-flavoured cousin of `for`/`sapply`. Works with any expression, not just a named function. ::: ## Functions compose into pipelines {.inv} The tidyverse pipes data through functions with `|>`: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} Pipe into your own function ```r penguins |> filter(!is.na(body_mass_g)) |> summarize(avg_mass = mean(body_mass_g)) # wrap a computation in your own function and pipe right in avg_mass_by <- function(df, group) { df |> filter(!is.na(body_mass_g)) |> group_by({{ group }}) |> summarize(avg_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)) } ``` ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **`{{ var }}`** is the tidyverse "embrace" shortcut that passes a bare column name into a function cleanly. We'll rely on it, and on writing tidy functions, throughout the Reproducible Workflows course. ::: ## Test your functions {.inv} A good habit: check a function against a case you *already know the answer to*: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} One-line assertions with `stopifnot` ```r stopifnot(f_to_c(32) == 0) # freezing stopifnot(f_to_c(212) == 100) # boiling stopifnot(all(clamp(c(-1, 0.5, 2)) == c(0, 0.5, 1))) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **Why it matters.** Writing one-line *assertions* (`stopifnot`) turns "trust me" into "checked automatically". You'll build on this with a proper testing framework in the Reproducible Workflows course. ::: ## Your turn: functions {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} 1. `zscore(x)` = `(x - mean(x)) / sd(x)`, tested on `c(1,2,3,4,5)`. 2. `mad_ratio(x)` = `mean(abs(x - mean(x))) / sd(x)`, tested on `rnorm(1000)`. 3. `describe(x)` → named list of `mean`, `sd`, `median`, `min`, `max`. 4. (Stretch) Wrap the matrices standardisation into `standardize_cols(M)` using `sweep`. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **Lab 3: functions (≈25 min).** Continue in `lab-3-functions.R`; the matrices standardisation in Q4 hands your `sweep` work a reusable home. ::: # Wrap up ## Three moves, one toolbox {.dark auto-animate=true background-color="#17251F"} ::: {.big-title data-id="title" style="left:88px; top:150px; width:720px; font-size:72px;"} Repeat, reach, package. ::: ::: {.panel data-id="draft" style="left:840px; top:150px; width:150px; height:360px;"} ::: ::: {.panel data-id="review" style="left:1006px; top:150px; width:150px; height:170px;"} ::: ::: {.panel data-id="release" style="left:1006px; top:340px; width:150px; height:170px;"} ::: ## Repeat, reach, package {.light auto-animate=true background-color="#F1EEE6"} ::: {.big-title data-id="title" style="left:92px; top:104px; width:1100px; font-size:44px;"} One toolbox for repetition & structure. ::: ::: {.panel .card data-id="draft" style="left:96px; top:220px; width:340px; height:360px;"} [Repeat & branch]{.h} [`for`/`while` to loop, `if/else` and `ifelse` to branch, `*apply` and pre-allocation for speed.]{.p} ::: ::: {.panel .card data-id="review" style="left:470px; top:220px; width:340px; height:360px;"} [Reach 2D with matrices]{.h} [One vector in two dimensions: build with `matrix`, do algebra with `%*%`/`solve`, summarise rows/columns with `apply` and `sweep`.]{.p} ::: ::: {.panel .card data-id="release" style="left:844px; top:220px; width:340px; height:360px;"} [Package the logic]{.h} [Turn repeated work into named, vectorised, tested functions: scope-aware, pipe-friendly, reusable.]{.p} ::: ## Your toolbox: `source()` your own `.R` {.light auto-animate=true background-color="#F1EEE6"} ::: {.big-title data-id="title" style="left:92px; top:104px; width:1100px; font-size:44px;"} From one-off script to a toolbox you keep. ::: ::: {.panel .card data-id="release" style="left:96px; top:200px; width:800px; height:400px;"} [Bundle the functions you wrote today]{.h} [Every function in this session (`clt_sim()`, `zscore()`, your loop and matrix helpers) is a tool. Drop them all into one file `my_tools.R` and `source("my_tools.R")` when an analysis needs them. That file is your first **toolbox**: a step toward a real package, and the exact artifact the Reproducible Workflows course picks up: `source()`d inside your Quarto reports, tracked by git, pinned by `renv`.]{.p style="font-size:24px; line-height:1.6;"} ::: ::: {.panel .marker data-id="draft" style="left:944px; top:230px;"} ::: ::: {.panel .marker data-id="review" style="left:944px; top:290px;"} ::: ## Next time {.dark .finale auto-animate=true background-color="#17251F"} ::: {.big-title data-id="title" style="left:240px; top:300px; width:800px; font-size:66px; text-align:center;"} Reproducible Workflows: Quarto, reports, git, and publishing. ::: ::: {.panel data-id="draft" style="left:470px; top:150px; width:110px; height:110px;"} ::: ::: {.panel data-id="review" style="left:590px; top:150px; width:110px; height:110px;"} ::: ::: {.panel data-id="release" style="left:710px; top:150px; width:110px; height:110px;"} ::: ::: {style="position:absolute; left:96px; top:600px; width:1024px; font-size:17px; color:rgba(241,238,230,0.62);"} Between sessions: finish any outstanding labs and collect your best functions into your `my_tools.R`. <script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
